slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code modifies the DOM by creating and inserting multiple absolutely positioned watermark text elements with configurable text, color, angle, and layout. It accesses and manipulates DOM elements and styles, removing existing watermarks before adding new ones, but does not perform any network, file, or system operations. This behavior facilitates UI watermarking for content protection without involving sensitive data access or exfiltration.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code implements a watermarking feature by dynamically creating and inserting styled text elements into the DOM to visually mark content. It does not perform any destructive DOM manipulation, does not access or exfiltrate sensitive data, nor does it execute or inject arbitrary code. Compared to the known malicious patterns, it lacks any sabotage logic (like blanking the page), unsanitized innerHTML assignments, or phishing overlays. The use of DOM manipulation and style injection is legitimate and expected for watermarking. There is no evidence of obfuscation, environment-based sabotage, or user credential theft. Therefore, it is very likely benign.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (when the web application loads in the browser), the code checks for the presence and value of the VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY environment variable and verifies if the application is running on a hardcoded list of allowed domains in production; if these checks fail, it sets document.body.innerHTML to an empty string, resulting in the entire web page being erased and the application rendered unusable for end users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs destructive actions by blanking the entire web page if the deployment environment does not meet specific, hardcoded criteria. This is not a standard practice and is indicative of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain logic that disables or destroys the application based on deployment environment or domain. Normal frontend code does not erase the UI for users based on environment variables or domain checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Domain and environment variable checks are sometimes used for licensing enforcement or feature gating, but legitimate implementations do not destroy the user interface or application functionality as a consequence.
key_indicators: Destructive DOM manipulation (document.body.innerHTML = '')
Hardcoded allow-list of domains in frontend code
Conditional logic tied to environment variables (VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY, NODE_ENV)
Sabotage logic triggered only in production environments
Absence of user notification or error handling before destructive action

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the web application is loaded in the browser)
execution_context.file_location: main JavaScript bundle (code injected by the package, typically in the entry point or a core module)

package_info.why_malicious: The package embeds code that intentionally sabotages web applications by erasing the UI if the app is deployed on domains not present in a hardcoded allow-list. This retaliatory logic is triggered in production environments and is designed to break unauthorized deployments, constituting a form of vigilante or destructive malware.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code is included in the web application via the @jayxuz/vue3-admin-icons npm package during the build process.
attack_chain.leads_to: The malicious logic becomes part of the deployed JavaScript bundle.

attack_chain.action: When the application is loaded in the browser, the injected code executes and checks the deployment environment, including environment variables and the current domain.
attack_chain.leads_to: The code determines if the application is running on an unauthorized domain in a production environment.

attack_chain.action: If the domain is not on the hardcoded allow-list and NODE_ENV is 'production', the code erases the web page content by setting document.body.innerHTML to an empty string.
attack_chain.leads_to: The application UI is destroyed, making the web app unusable for end users on unauthorized domains.

behavioral_signatures: Frontend JavaScript code that checks document.domain against a hardcoded allow-list
Destructive DOM manipulation such as setting document.body.innerHTML to an empty string
Conditional sabotage logic based on environment variables (e.g., VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY, NODE_ENV)
Sabotage actions triggered only in production environments
file_indicators: JavaScript files containing checks for document.domain against specific domains: 'localhost', 'chu1204505056.gitee.io', '127.0.0.1', 'vue-admin-beautiful.com'
References to VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY and NODE_ENV in frontend code
Presence of code that sets document.body.innerHTML = ''
network_indicators: None (the code does not perform any network communication or exfiltration in this snippet)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Automated scanners should analyze JavaScript bundles for hardcoded domain allow-lists combined with destructive DOM actions, such as setting document.body.innerHTML to an empty string. Flag any package or code that erases the UI based on environment variables or production checks. Review for the presence of sabotage logic that disables the application outside of specific domains, especially when tied to environment variables like VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY and NODE_ENV.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (web page rendering), the code creates a DOM element and assigns unsanitized user input directly to its innerHTML property, resulting in the injection of arbitrary HTML or JavaScript into the page, which can lead to cross-site scripting (XSS) and execution of attacker-controlled scripts in the user's browser.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly assigning user input to innerHTML without any sanitization or escaping allows attackers to inject malicious scripts, a classic XSS vulnerability.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: User input should always be sanitized or escaped before being rendered as HTML to prevent script injection; this code fails to do so.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rendering trusted, pre-sanitized content or using textContent for user input to avoid HTML interpretation.
key_indicators: Direct assignment of user input to innerHTML
Absence of input sanitization or escaping
Creation of DOM elements with user-controlled content

package_info.why_malicious: The report highlights the presence of critical software vulnerabilities, as defined by the CWE Top 10 for 2021, which, if present in code, can be exploited for malicious purposes. These include vulnerabilities such as unchecked memory allocation, improper input validation, and unsanitized DOM manipulation, leading to risks like remote code execution, data exfiltration, privilege escalation, and unauthorized access. The focus is on dangerous coding patterns and insecure practices rather than a specific package.

attack_chain.action: Attacker provides crafted input to exploit memory allocation or input validation flaws, such as oversized values or non-decimal IP formats.
attack_chain.leads_to: Memory corruption, arbitrary code execution, or bypass of input validation, enabling further exploitation.

attack_chain.action: Attacker injects malicious script or payload via unsanitized user input into the DOM.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser (XSS), session hijacking, or further exploitation.

behavioral_signatures: Unchecked user input used in memory allocation or pointer arithmetic without bounds checking
Direct assignment of user input to innerHTML or other DOM properties without sanitization
Input validation functions that only check for decimal values and do not reject octal or hexadecimal input
file_indicators: C++ files with custom operator new implementations lacking input size validation
JavaScript files with direct innerHTML assignments from user input
JavaScript input parsing functions that use parseInt with a fixed radix and lack comprehensive format checks
network_indicators: Unusual outbound connections or crashes following memory corruption events
Unexpected HTTP requests or script execution triggered by XSS payloads
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Use static analysis tools to identify unchecked memory allocations, pointer arithmetic with user input, direct DOM assignments from user input, and input validation functions that do not handle all input formats. Monitor runtime for abnormal memory access patterns, DOM-based XSS attempts, and unexpected network activity following user input processing. Correlate code patterns with runtime behaviors to identify exploitation attempts.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code creates and injects a DOM overlay element into the webpage, presenting a prompt for the user to connect their crypto wallet or scan a QR code. This overlay captures user interaction and can redirect sensitive wallet credentials or session data to attacker-controlled infrastructure, resulting in potential credential theft or wallet compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The injection of a UI overlay that solicits sensitive actions, such as connecting a crypto wallet or scanning a QR code, is a hallmark of phishing attacks. This behavior is highly anomalous for an animation rendering library and is designed to deceive users into divulging credentials or authorizing malicious transactions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate @lottiefiles/lottie-player package should only provide animation rendering capabilities and never prompt users for wallet connections, display overlays unrelated to animation, or interact with cryptocurrency features.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate wallet connection prompts are only expected in cryptocurrency wallet extensions or decentralized applications (dApps), not in generic animation libraries like lottie-player. Any such prompt in this context is highly suspicious.
key_indicators: JavaScript code that creates and injects DOM overlays unrelated to animation playback
UI elements containing wallet connection prompts or QR codes in a non-crypto package
References to wallet connection, QR code images, or external resources not associated with lottiefiles.com
Overlay elements styled or positioned to capture user attention and solicit sensitive actions

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the lottie-player component is loaded in the browser)
required_permissions: network access (if wallet connection or QR code interaction triggers external requests)

package_info.why_malicious: These versions were published by attackers who compromised the package's NPM automation token, allowing them to inject malicious JavaScript that displays a deceptive UI overlay. This overlay prompts users to connect their cryptocurrency wallets or scan a QR code, which can result in credential theft or unauthorized wallet access. Such behavior is entirely unrelated to the legitimate purpose of an animation player library and constitutes a targeted phishing attack.

attack_chain.action: Attacker obtains a leaked NPM automation token and uses it to publish trojanized versions (2.0.5, 2.0.6, 2.0.7) of @lottiefiles/lottie-player to the npm registry.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious package versions become available for installation via npm.

attack_chain.action: Developers or users unknowingly install the compromised package versions as dependencies in their projects.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is included in application bundles and loaded in user environments.

attack_chain.action: When the affected lottie-player component is loaded in a browser, the malicious code executes and injects a deceptive UI overlay prompting users to connect their crypto wallets or scan a QR code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Users may interact with the overlay, resulting in credential theft or unauthorized wallet access if sensitive information is submitted.

behavioral_signatures: DOM overlays injected at runtime by animation libraries, especially those prompting for crypto wallet connections
Presence of wallet connect buttons or QR code prompts in UI elements rendered by non-crypto packages
JavaScript code in animation libraries that manipulates the DOM to display overlays unrelated to animation playback
file_indicators: Overlay injection code present in dist/lottie-player.js or main JavaScript bundle
References to wallet connection, QR code images (e.g., 'malicious-qr.png'), or external domains not associated with lottiefiles.com
Unexpected HTML or JavaScript code for wallet prompts in package source files
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP(S) requests to domains or endpoints not affiliated with lottiefiles.com, especially those related to wallet connection or credential submission
Loading of external images or scripts (such as QR codes) from suspicious or unrecognized domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Perform static and dynamic analysis of animation library packages to identify DOM manipulations that inject overlays or prompt for wallet connections. Flag any code in @lottiefiles/lottie-player that references wallet connection, QR codes, or external domains unrelated to animation rendering. Monitor for unexpected UI changes in applications using this package. Use automated scanning to detect overlay injection patterns and review network activity for connections to suspicious domains or endpoints.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, on page load or script execution, the code injects external scripts into the page, including a deprecated version of Ionicons and a remote script (slim.js) hosted on jsDelivr, which itself contains the trojanized jQuery. This enables further malicious code execution and persistence by loading additional payloads from attacker-controlled sources.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script injects remote code from attacker-controlled sources without user consent, using a misleading deprecation warning to disguise its activity and facilitate further compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not inject remote scripts or downgrade libraries without explicit user action or clear documentation. Core libraries should not dynamically load external code from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script injection is used in some legitimate plugin loaders, but not in core libraries or without user awareness and explicit opt-in.
key_indicators: Injection of remote scripts from suspicious or attacker-controlled domains
Phony deprecation warnings in console output to mislead users
Use of outdated or deprecated library versions
Chaining to further malicious payloads via dynamic script loading

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, on page load or script execution

package_info.package_versions: 8.0.0 (and dozens of others, see report for full list)
package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a trojanized version of jQuery in which the 'end' prototype function is maliciously modified to exfiltrate all form data from the page to attacker-controlled domains whenever it is called, either directly or indirectly (e.g., via fadeTo). The package is distributed under many names and versions, often with additional suspicious files and unique exfiltration URLs, indicating a persistent, manually assembled supply chain attack targeting web applications.

attack_chain.action: User installs a malicious npm package containing a trojanized jQuery file (or similar).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is present in the project and loaded in the browser.

attack_chain.action: Trojanized jQuery is loaded and used in the web application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious prototype function (end) is available in the global jQuery object.

attack_chain.action: User or application code calls fadeTo or end (directly or indirectly), triggering the malicious end function.
attack_chain.leads_to: Form data is serialized and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled domains.

attack_chain.action: Injected scripts (from icons.js/min.js) load additional remote payloads (e.g., slim.js) from jsDelivr, which may contain further trojanized code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and further compromise of the web application.

behavioral_signatures: Modification of jQuery prototype functions (especially end) to perform network requests
Exfiltration of serialized form data via AJAX to external domains
Dynamic injection of remote scripts from non-standard or outdated sources
Presence of phony deprecation warnings in console output
file_indicators: jquery.min.js, registration.min.js, icon.min.js, fontawesome.js, slim.js, all-min.js (with non-standard or unexpected content)
Presence of termux.properties, npm cache, or npm logs in package tarballs
network_indicators: Requests to domains such as *.truex.biz.id, *.hanznesia.my.id, *.api-system.engineer, *.jsdelivr.net/gh/indexsc/libs/slim.js, and other listed campaign domains
AJAX GET requests with hex-encoded form data in query parameters
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan JavaScript dependencies for modifications to core library prototype functions (e.g., jQuery.fn.end). Flag any code that serializes and exfiltrates form data to external domains. Monitor for dynamic script injection from non-standard or outdated sources, and alert on requests to known campaign domains. Review package contents for unexpected files (e.g., termux.properties, npm logs) and non-standard file naming patterns. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify supply chain attacks.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime in the browser, the injected code appends a script tag with src set to https://send.wagateway.pro/client.js?cache=ignore to the DOM, causing the browser to fetch and execute additional malicious JavaScript from the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is obfuscated and mass-injected into all JavaScript files, ensuring that every page load triggers the download and execution of untrusted code from an external domain controlled by the attacker.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code should not inject remote scripts from unrelated or untrusted domains into all JavaScript files, especially using obfuscation and without user or developer consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script loading is sometimes used for analytics or feature toggles, but not in an obfuscated, repository-wide, and externally controlled manner.
key_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript injected into all *.js files
Dynamically creates a script tag with src pointing to send.wagateway.pro/client.js
No legitimate business logic—sole purpose is to load further code from an attacker-controlled domain
Script tag uses a unique id (hook-loader) to avoid duplicate injection

execution_context.trigger: At runtime in the browser when any modified JavaScript file is loaded
execution_context.file_location: assets/js/*.js (appended to the end of every JavaScript file in the repository)

package_info.package_manager: GitHub (malicious commit, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (affects repositories via commit, not a package release)
package_info.why_malicious: The attack involves unauthorized commits impersonating Dependabot, introducing a malicious GitHub Actions workflow and modifying all JavaScript files to exfiltrate repository secrets and end-user credentials. The entire commit is malicious, targeting both developer and user security by stealing secrets and injecting credential-stealing code.

attack_chain.action: Attacker obtains a developer's GitHub personal access token (PAT), likely via a separate malicious package or phishing.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to authenticate as the victim and push code to their repositories.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses the stolen PAT to commit malicious code to the victim's repositories, impersonating Dependabot to avoid suspicion.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is introduced into the repository under the guise of a trusted automation tool.

attack_chain.action: A malicious GitHub Actions workflow is added to exfiltrate repository secrets and variables on every push event.
attack_chain.leads_to: Repository secrets and variables are sent to the attacker's command and control (C2) server.

attack_chain.action: All JavaScript files in the repository are modified to append an obfuscated script loader that fetches additional malicious code from an external domain.
attack_chain.leads_to: End-users of the web application are exposed to further malicious payloads when they load the compromised JavaScript files.

attack_chain.action: The loaded remote script intercepts password form submissions in the browser and exfiltrates credentials to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: End-user credentials are stolen and sent to the attacker's C2 server, achieving the attacker's final objective.

behavioral_signatures: Addition or modification of GitHub Actions workflows that POST repository secrets or variables to external domains
Mass modification of JavaScript (*.js) files to append obfuscated script loaders
JavaScript code that dynamically injects script tags with src pointing to suspicious external domains
Client-side code that intercepts password form submissions and sends serialized form data to untrusted endpoints
file_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript code appended to the end of assets/js/*.js files
Presence of script tags with id 'hook-loader' and src set to send.wagateway.pro/client.js
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified GitHub Actions workflows that serialize and POST secrets or variables to external domains. Scan for mass changes to JavaScript files, especially for obfuscated code that injects remote scripts from send.wagateway.pro. Detect client-side code that attaches event listeners to password forms and exfiltrates credentials. Flag any network traffic to send.wagateway.pro domains as a high-confidence indicator of compromise.
